note: In Dante's poem the canto opens with the hymn itself, three lines mixing Latin and Hebrew words: "Hosanna, holy God of hosts". The translation begins just after it.

context: He has finished the long speech of Canto 6 and goes back to the dance. "Substance" is the philosophers' word for a being that exists in its own right, here a soul.

note: Not explained, and much debated. Common readings are his two glories as emperor and lawgiver, or his own light joined to the light of God's grace.

context: Dante has a question and is too much in awe of her to ask it. She reads it in his mind, and her answer fills the rest of the canto.

note: Dante's Italian says the reverence masters him "by Be and by ice": the mere syllables of her name are enough. Bice was the everyday short form of Beatrice.
Her smile would make a man happy even while he burned.

Justinian's riddle in Canto 6: the Crucifixion was a just punishment for Adam's sin, yet the destruction of Jerusalem justly punished those who carried it out. If the first was just, why was anyone punished for it?

quote: that man who was never born
context: Made directly by God, not born of a mother. His sin was to refuse the one limit set on him, and it passed to all his descendants: original sin.

note: God the Son, called the Word in the opening of John's Gospel. His descent is the Incarnation: God taking on human nature and being born as Jesus.
The Church's teaching that Christ is one person with two natures, wholly God and wholly man. This is the doctrine Justinian said he once doubted (Canto 6). Beatrice's answer depends on it.

quote: pure and good as when first made
note: The human nature Christ took was free of sin, as Adam's was at his creation. But human nature in itself, in the next lines, was guilty and exiled from Eden.

The solution. Look at the human nature that suffered on the cross, and no punishment was ever more just, since that nature had sinned in Adam. Look at the divine person who bore it, and none was ever more unjust.

quote: pleased both God and the Jews
note: For opposite reasons: God willed the death as the redemption of mankind, and those who demanded it acted from malice. This is the medieval Christian view that held the Jews of Jerusalem guilty of Christ's death.

quote: made earth tremble and heaven open
note: The Gospel of Matthew tells of an earthquake at the moment Christ died. Heaven, closed to mankind since Adam, was opened by the same death.
Rome. Its army under Titus destroyed Jerusalem in AD 70, which Dante treats as a lawful sentence carried out by the Empire.
Dante's second, unspoken question: why did God redeem mankind by so terrible a means? Beatrice's answer follows the reasoning of Anselm of Canterbury's Why God Became Man, written just before 1100.
Reasoning alone will not reach this mystery. It is understood only by a mind grown up in love.
God keeps nothing back out of jealousy. Creation is his goodness overflowing, an idea that goes back to Plato and reached Dante through Boethius.

What God makes with his own hand, with nothing in between, has three gifts: it lasts forever, it is free of the influence of the stars, and it resembles him. Everything else is made through the workings of nature.
A legal word: the rights of a free citizen. Sin makes mankind less like God and so forfeits the privileges it was created with.
All human nature was present in Adam, its seed, so all of it sinned when he did and lost Eden with him.
The two ways back. Either God simply forgives, which is mercy, or man pays the debt in full, which is justice.
The debt could not be paid by man. Adam's pride aimed at being equal to God ("you shall be as gods", Genesis 3), and no creature can humble itself as far down as that reached up.
Mercy and justice. God used both: he had mercy by becoming man himself, and as a man he paid what justice required.

quote: between first day and final night
note: From the Creation to the Last Judgment, the whole of time.
The heart of the answer. A free pardon would have left mankind passive. By becoming man, God let humanity itself make good its fault, a greater gift than forgiveness alone.
The four elements of which, in ancient and medieval science, everything under the Moon is made. All such things decay. Dante's objection: if what God creates lasts forever, why do these perish?
The angels and the heavens were created directly by God, complete as they are, and so they do not decay.
"Informed" in the philosophers' sense: given their form. God made the raw matter of the elements, but the things made from it are shaped by other created things, the stars, and so they can perish.

quote: The soul of every animal and plant
note: The life of plants and beasts is drawn out of matter by the light and motion of the stars. It is not made directly by God, and dies with the body.

The human soul is the exception: God creates each one himself, as he "breathed the breath of life" into Adam (Genesis 2). So it is immortal and longs for him. Statius explained the same thing in Purgatorio 25.

A last proof. God formed the bodies of Adam and Eve directly too, so the human body was also meant to last forever. Death came in with sin, and the body will be restored at the resurrection at the end of time.
